Illinois Corn Growers Association appreciates the opportunity to provide comments supporting the 

Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS). Congress passed this Standard in 2005 and again in 2007 to help 

the U.S. move to a source of cleaner burning, domestically produced fuel that benefits the environment 

and moves America towards energy independence. Those same goals are still of the utmost 

importance today. 

We must preserve the RFS and congressional intent of the RFS to achieve these increasingly important 

goals. 

Congress intended the RFS to challenge both the biofuels industry and the petroleum industry to 

produce more biofuels and to blend more biofuels in the fuel markets. The blend wall was never viewed 

as a barrier to increased demand by Congress. We need EPA to continue pushing demand and 

production of biofuels through the RFS according to the statutes. The system has worked relatively well 

under your Administration for corn-based ethanol. The industry now has the capacity to produce 16 

billion gallons of ethanol with a maximum RFS allowance of 15 billion. 

The opportunity is now with the U.S. EPA to better synchronize two major programs that impact the 

petroleum industry, the ethanol industry, marketers, autos, agriculture and most importantly consumers 

for the benefit of all. 

The future of the RFS depends on growing demand AND production. The proposed CAFÉ and GHG 

emissions standards in the future would grow a very cost-effective demand for biofuels if engines were 

synchronized with high octane fuels using mid-level blends of ethanol. Certain regulatory barriers 

under EPA’s control would have to be lifted, but the two programs would then work together to reach 

similar goals of reducing petroleum use, reducing GHG emissions and building a sustainable market for 

biofuels. 

Attached are the comments submitted by the National Corn Growers Association and additional 

comments from Illinois and Missouri Corn Growers further describing some of the actions needed to 

make this happen. We would be pleased to discuss these comments further.

The State of Colorado submits these comments in response to the U.S. Environmental 
Protection Agency’s (“EPA’s”) proposed rule: “Updating Regulations on Water Quality 
Certification,” 40 CFR Part 121, as published in the Federal Register on August 22, 2019. 84 
Fed. Reg. 44080 (“EPA Proposal”). 
 
EPA is proposing a complete overhaul of its longstanding regulations, which serve as the 
“umbrella” regulatory framework to implement Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (“CWA” or 
“the Act”). EPA’s proposal drastically undermines the tenets of cooperative federalism in the 
CWA and inappropriately encroaches into authority expressly reserved to the states and 
authorized tribes (hereinafter referred to as “certifying authorities” or “states”) under 
Section 401, 33 U.S.C. § 1341. As recognized by Congress, states are in the best position to 
protect their waterways through their own individualized water quality certification processes 
that are tailored to work within their own legal frameworks, especially when certifications 
cross into the realm of water allocation and management. See 33 U.S.C. § 1251(b); 33 U.S.C. 
§ 1341; 33 U.S.C. § 1370. Colorado is concerned about the impacts that EPA’s proposal, if 
finalized, will have on our ability to protect the quality of Colorado’s valuable water 
resources in the context of essential water storage and supply infrastructure projects. We 
want to ensure that EPA considers the implications of the proposed rule changes for these 
critical water supply projects, which are somewhat unique to Colorado, and which are very 
different from the energy infrastructure projects that are a main driver of EPA’s proposal per 
the directives in Executive Order 13868, Promoting Energy Infrastructure and Economic 
Growth. 84 Fed. Reg. 15,495 (Apr. 15, 2019).

(“Rollover Rule”). This request is submitted by New Flyer of America Inc. (NFA), which makes transit

As explained below, NFA respectfully asks NHTSA to clarify and refine this definition, so that physically

Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
The National Hydropower Association (NHA) submits the following comments on EPA’s 
proposed Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule (the 
Proposed Rule).1 NHA is joined in these comments by the Northwest Hydroelectric Association 
(NWHA). 
 
The Proposed Rule would substantially replace the Section 401 certification rule that EPA 
adopted only two years ago (the 2020 Rule).2 The 2020 Rule itself replaced rules that had not 
been substantially revised since before the 1972 enactment of the Clean Water Act (CWA) and 
that were based on a significantly different statute that preceded Section 401. The long failure to 
update the rules allowed the accumulation of many problems related to the interpretation and 
application of Section 401, which negatively affected the hydropower industry and its ability to 
implement projects needed to address critical environmental and energy issues, including climate 
change. 
 
Before adopting the Proposed Rule, EPA should carefully consider the problems that the 2020 
Rule was intended to address and whether the Proposed Rule would resurrect those problems, 
particularly for the licensing of hydropower projects that will be essential to meet the urgent 
need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. NHA and NWHA urge EPA to retain the 2020 Rule 
without substantial revisions because it effectively addresses the problems that predated it while 
adhering closely to the text and purposes of Section 401. If, however, EPA chooses to move 
forward with the Proposed Rule, these comments suggest revisions to reduce the risk of re-
creating or exacerbating the problems resolved by the 2020 Rule.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on NPRM, 85 Fed. Reg. 23266. The 
Disability Law Center (DLC) is Utah’s Protection and Advocacy (P&A) system and Client

CAP, we advise people with disabilities of the services available to them under the 
Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and advocate for the rights of people with disabilities in their 
relationships with these programs. The DLC reviewed the Department of Education’s NPRM, 85 
Fed. Reg. 23266, April 27, 2020, entitled “Proposed Priorities—Innovative Rehabilitation 
Training Program.” We submit the following comment, specific to Proposed Priority 1, 
“Innovative Rehabilitation Training Project, Client Assistance Program.” 
 
The proposed approach in Priority 1, which is similar to that described in Priorities 2 and 3 
governing the vocational rehabilitation training program, will not adequately meet the needs of 
CAP programs. The training needs of CAP staff are distinct from the beneficiaries of the other 
proposed priorities. CAP programs provide advocacy to clients of VR who may be experiencing 
disagreements with the services the VR program has provided, making the proposed approach in 
Priority 1 ineffective. The DLC does not see a need to merge the CAP training program with an 
academic program for VR professionals. The roles played by VR and CAP staff are distinct, one 
of counselor and one of legal advocate, and require very different training and skillsets. The CAP 
program, as the advocate for VR clients, may even have conflicting purposes and goals with the 
VR program. For example, the DLC’s CAP program has advocated for a broader interpretation 
of state VR policies when not in alignment with federal regulations. Although there is a need for 
some cross-training on VR services for CAP staff, joining these distinct entities for training 
purposes could damage the integrity of the programs.

In reading the proposal, for the reclassification of Stephens' Kangaroo Rat, I find a contradiction which needs to be addressed, before a decision can be made. The proposal summary, clearly states, "This proposed action is based on a thorough review of the best scientific and commercial data available, which indicates that the Stephens' kangaroo rat no longer meets the definition of endangered under the Act.". This statement suggests that all scientific and commercial data available is complete and accurate. Furthermore, it is stated under the section labeled Species Report for Stephens' Kangaroo Rat that, "a species report, which includes a thorough review of the species' taxonomy, natural history, habitats, ecology, population, range and threats facing the species or its habitat to assist us in determining the status of the species.", was used to determine whether a reclassification from endangered to threatened was warranted. The proposal goes on to say under the Population Trend and Demographic Information section that, "Exact population trends and density estimates for the Stephens' kangaroo rat are not determinable at this time given the incomplete surveys of all potentially occupied areas and variable information collected during those surveys.". These statements, in my opinion contradict each other. The population data is incomplete, as stated previously in the proposal. One cannot base this proposed action on contradicting information. I believe that this proposal needs to be reviewed before any other action is taken. The population data/survey results need to be completed before a decision can be reached on reclassifying the Stephens' kangaroo rat from endangered to threatened. Once the completed population data/surveys are reviewed, if at that time, the data suggested the population has increased to an adequate level, then reclassification would be warranted. For the above-mentioned contradiction, I am opposed to this rule. If a reclassification from endangered to threaten is warranted, I am pleased to know that the habitat areas will continue to be protected for the foreseeable future, to ensure the population levels remain well above the threshold for endangered species status.

I strongly SUPPORT the proposed critical habitat protections for the five threatened Caribbean coral species and seven threatened Indo-Pacific coral species. 

All of these species have undergone some level of population decline and are susceptible to multiple threats. Notably, the most severe threats are attributed to climate change which NMFS describes as creating a foreseeable likelihood and danger of extinction for these corals throughout all of their ranges. 

An estimated 50% of coral reefs worldwide have already been lost to climate change, and about one-third of reef-building coral species are at risk of extinction. Stressors and risks to threatened coral species include both climate related threats as well as ecological effects of fishing and land-based sources of pollution. 

Impacts of the climate crisis include ocean acidification, which hinders the ability of corals to grow, and ocean warming, which causes corals to expel the algae living in their tissues in a phenomenon known as coral bleaching. 

High-growth conditions for reef-building corals include clear, warm waters with abundant light, and low levels of nutrients, sediments, and freshwater. Critical habitat designations are necessary to reduce and remove threats to these conditions which foster growth and recovery of these threatened species

Coral reefs help support over 25% of all marine life, and designation of critical habitat for these coral species means a chance for recovery and the opportunity to save them from extinction.
